chapter.name: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

questions.q: Arjun asks, 'Why are there so many shapes of leaves?' and stops there. Kavya asks, 'Do leaves of the same plant grow larger in shade than in sunlight?' and plans to compare plants kept in both places. Which statement best describes Kavya's step, as the chapter sees it?
questions.a: She moved from a simple why question to a focused question she can test
o: She moved from a simple why question to a focused question she can test
She stayed at the wonder stage, asking a simple why question like Arjun
She showed that a scientific answer, once found, never changes later
She replaced careful observation with free imagination about leaves

questions.q: For three weeks, Tanvi carefully writes down the time her neighbour's dough takes to rise each morning, but she never suggests any idea about what might change it or what to try next. Which lesson of the book's page symbols is her work missing?
questions.a: The kite: curiosity must take flight with creative thinking
o: The kite: curiosity must take flight with creative thinking
The root: staying grounded in careful, real observations
Both: she has neither observed carefully nor imagined anything
Neither: careful records alone are a complete investigation

questions.q: True or False? 'A question such as "Is the world getting warmer?" is too big for young investigators; the chapter keeps investigation to small kitchen puzzles.' Give the verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the real-world puzzles young scientists explore may range from everyday life, like why dough rises, to the bigger mysteries of Earth and beyond, like whether the world is getting warmer.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: puzzles range from everyday ones to bigger mysteries such as the world getting warmer

questions.q: Which of these best shows a student 'using observations to improve understanding'?
questions.a: Sana fried three thicknesses of dough and changed her guess after seeing them
o: Sana fried three thicknesses of dough and changed her guess after seeing them
Sana read that dough rises, wrote the sentence in her notebook and learnt it by heart
Sana wrote 'Why does dough rise?' on a chart paper and pinned it on the class board
Sana drew a large kite in her notebook to remind herself to think creatively

questions.q:
Four lines from Meghna's investigation notebook got mixed up:
P: 'So hotter oil seemed to make the puri puff sooner in my trials.'
Q: 'Does the temperature of the oil change how fast a puri puffs?'
R: 'Fried one puri each in hot and not very hot oil and timed them.'
S: 'Hot oil: 4 seconds; not very hot oil: 11 seconds.'
The chapter says we use questions as starting points to observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully and explain clearly. Put the lines in that order and say which line is the starting question and which is the conclusion drawn from the observations.
questions.a: Order: Q, R, S, P. Q is the starting question; R is the experiment done thoughtfully; S is the careful observation; P is the conclusion drawn from what was observed.
s: Correct order Q, R, S, P
Q identified as the starting question
P identified as the conclusion drawn from the observations

questions.q:
A teacher sets two homework tasks.
Task P: Copy ten facts about microbes from the textbook into your notebook.
Task Q: Keep two bowls of the same milk with the same starter, one in a warm place and one in a cool place, and note which sets into curd first.
The chapter says, 'We don't want you to just learn new facts, we want you to learn how to find new facts.' Which task matches this aim? Give a reason.
questions.a: Task Q. It asks a focused question, uses a simple experiment and an observation to find something out, which is learning how to find new facts. Task P only collects facts someone else has already found.
s: Chooses Task Q
Reason: Q finds out by experiment and observation; P only copies known facts

questions.q:
At a school science fair in Pune, judges have one prize for 'the best example of investigation'. The prize rule says the project must include an experiment done this year with its observations recorded.
Project | What the team did
P | Asked 'Why are there so many kinds of insects?' and displayed 40 sharp photos of insects found near the school
Q | Asked 'Does curd set faster in a steel bowl or a clay pot?'; used the same milk and starter in both and checked every hour
R | Last year found that mustard seeds sprout on wet cotton; this year wrote the new question 'Does the amount of water matter?' but has not started the experiment
S | Made a chart of ten facts about the Moon copied from books
(a) Which project shows the Grade 7 idea that an answer opens a new question?
(b) For Project Q, what did the team change and what did it observe?
(c) Project P has careful photos. Why is it still not an investigation in the chapter's sense?
(d) Decide which project should win the prize, using your answers above and the prize rule.
questions.a: (a) Project R: last year's answer led to a new question. (b) Changed: the type of bowl (steel or clay); observed: the time the curd took to set. (c) P asked a simple why question and observed, but did not ask a focused question or design an experiment to answer it. (d) Project Q. It has a focused question, a simple experiment with other conditions kept the same and recorded observations, so it meets the rule; R has not done this year's experiment, P has no experiment, and S only copies facts.
s: Part (a): Project R
Part (b): changed bowl type; observed setting time
Part (c): P has no focused question or experiment, only observation
Part (d): Project Q, with reasons rejecting R, P and S against the rule

questions.q:
Kabir's project log for one week reads:
Mon: 'I wonder why some seeds sprout faster than others.'
Tue: 'Question: do mustard seeds sprout sooner on wet cotton or on dry cotton?'
Wed: 'Kept 10 seeds on wet cotton and 10 on dry cotton on the same window sill.'
Sat: 'Wet cotton: 8 sprouted; dry cotton: 0. Question answered for good. Project closed.'
(a) Which line is Grade 6-style wonder, and which line turns it into a focused question?
(b) Which lines keep the project grounded like the root, and why?
(c) His last line says 'answered for good'. Which Grade 7 idea does this go against? Explain.
(d) Write a Sunday line that lets the project take flight like the kite.
(e) Judge whether his week, as written, is a balanced investigation in the book's sense.
questions.a: (a) Monday's line is the wonder; Tuesday's line is the focused question. (b) Wednesday and Saturday: they record a real set-up and real, careful observations (the counts 8 and 0), which is the solid ground of observation. (c) The Grade 7 idea that science is always evolving and each answer opens new questions; his result should lead on to new questions, not close the project. (d) For example: 'Sunday: maybe the amount of water matters too; next week I will compare cotton that is just damp with cotton that is soaked.' (e) Not yet balanced: the focused question, the experiment and the observations give it strong roots, but closing the project stops his ideas from soaring and ignores that answers open new questions.
s: (a) Monday as wonder, Tuesday as focused question
(b) Wednesday and Saturday as real observations (root)
(c) goes against science evolving: answers open new questions
(d) a Sunday line with a new idea or question
(e) judgement: strong root, but closing the project leaves out the kite

questions.q:
A Class 8 science club in Nagpur is painting a banner for its first investigation of the year. Three mottos are on the shortlist.
Motto 1: 'Trust only what you can see and measure.'
Motto 2: 'Let your ideas fly wherever they want.'
Motto 3: 'Feet on the ground, ideas in the sky.'
The club secretary, Rohan, wants Motto 1 because 'imagination only leads to mistakes'.
(a) Decide which motto fits the chapter's view of how investigation works best, and give one reason.
(b) Which of the book's two page symbols matches Motto 1, and what does that symbol stand for?
(c) Which symbol matches Motto 2, and what does it remind us?
(d) Rohan says imagination only leads to mistakes. From the puri investigation, show one place where creative thinking is needed before any observing can even begin.
questions.a: (a) Motto 3. The chapter says investigation works best only when we balance the solid ground of careful observation with the freedom of creative thinking; Motto 3 holds both. (b) The root, printed at the bottom of left-hand pages: a deep, solid foundation of knowledge that keeps us grounded in real observations. (c) The kite, soaring in the top corner of right-hand pages: curiosity must take flight if we are to explore the unknown. (d) Before frying, someone has to imagine what all could be changed: different flours (atta, maida), a different thickness or size of dough, or new ways of putting the dough in (dropping it vertically, sliding it at an angle, sliding it slowly). Imagining these possibilities is creative thinking; without it the club would have nothing new to test, so Motto 1 alone would stall the investigation.
s: Part (a): Motto 3, because the chapter wants careful observation balanced with creative thinking
Part (b): root; solid foundation, staying grounded in real observations
Part (c): kite; curiosity must take flight to explore the unknown
Part (d): imagining what could be changed (flour, thickness, way of dropping) needs creative thinking before observing

questions.q:
Meena guessed that thinner dough would always puff faster. Her own record, using the same flour, the same oil and the same way of sliding the dough in:
2 mm thick: 5 s to puff; 4 mm thick: 5 s to puff; 6 mm thick: 5 s to puff.
(a) What does her record show about her guess?
(b) What does the book's idea of investigation say she should now do with her guess?
questions.a: (a) In her trials the time to puff stayed 5 s for all three thicknesses, so her own observations do not support the guess. (b) The book says investigators use their observations to improve their understanding, so she should change her idea instead of keeping it, and let this answer open a new question to test next (for example, whether the oil temperature changes the time).
s: Part (a): time stayed 5 s for every thickness, so the guess is not supported
Part (b): revise the idea using the observations and move to a new question

questions.q: In this book, every left-hand page has an even number and every right-hand page an odd number. Riya reads every page from page 54 to page 62, both included. The number of pages on which she sees the symbol that reminds us that curiosity must take flight is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

Kunal's science diary lists ten ideas, such as 'maybe music helps plants grow' and 'maybe moonlight makes them taller', but he has never measured or recorded anything about a real plant.
(a) Which of the book's two page symbols is his diary following, and which one is it missing?
(b) Pick one of his ideas and say what he must record, and how, to bring in the missing symbol.
questions.a: (a) It follows the kite (ideas taking flight, creative thinking) but misses the root (staying grounded in careful, real observations). (b) For example, for moonlight: keep two similar plants, one where moonlight falls at night and one covered at night, and measure each plant's height in cm every few days. Careful records like these ground his idea in real observation.
s: Part (a): follows the kite, misses the root
Part (b): one idea with a real observation or measurement to record

questions.q: Neha says, 'A careful observer should keep her own ideas out of an experiment, or her guesses will spoil what she sees. So while experimenting only the root matters; the kite can wait until the work is over.' Is she right? Explain using what the book says about its two page symbols.
questions.a: No. The book says the root and the kite together invite us to stay grounded in real observations while allowing our ideas to soar, and that investigation works best only when careful observation is balanced with creative thinking. Ideas are needed during the work too: they suggest what to change and what new question to ask after a round of trials. Observing carefully (root) does not mean switching off ideas (kite).
s: Verdict: she is not right
The two symbols are meant to work together, balancing observation and creative thinking
Ideas are needed during the work: what to change, what to ask next

questions.q: Last year Ishaan explained the Moon's changing shape one way. After reading more, he now explains it differently and expects his idea may change again. Which stage of the Curiosity journey does his experience show most directly?
questions.a: Grade 7: science keeps evolving and answers open new questions
o: Grade 7: science keeps evolving and answers open new questions
Grade 6: science begins with wonder and simple why questions
Grade 8: a focused question is tested by a simple experiment
None: a changed answer shows that the first idea was not science

questions.q: Before testing puris, Pooja notes down how her grandmother has always made puris for festivals. Then she plans to test whether Grandma's tip, 'slide the dough in slowly', really helps a puri puff. How do the book's two page symbols apply to her two steps?
questions.a: Grandma's way draws on the root; daring to test it lets the kite fly
o: Grandma's way draws on the root; daring to test it lets the kite fly
Grandma's way is the kite, since old family ideas are what let us soar
Testing the tip breaks the root, which means ideas we must never change
Only the root applies, since both steps are about the family's tradition

questions.q: Write two questions about a phulka swelling on a flame: one that only wonders (Grade 6 style) and one focused question that could be investigated with a simple experiment (Grade 8 style). For the second question, say what you would change and what you would observe.
questions.a: Example: Wonder question: 'Why does a phulka swell like a balloon?' Focused question: 'Does a thinner phulka swell faster on the flame than a thicker one?' Change: the thickness of the rolled dough (keeping flame and flour the same). Observe: whether it swells and the time it takes in seconds.
s: A simple why or how question
A focused, testable question
Names what is changed and what is observed for it

questions.q: 'In Grade 8, wonder and evolution come together to form the heart of how science works.' Justify this statement in five points: say what each of Grade 6 and Grade 7 contributed, what investigation adds, why the book wants investigators and not only learners, and give one example of a real-world puzzle from the chapter.
questions.a: (1) Grade 6 showed that science begins with wonder, with simple 'Why?' and 'How?' questions. (2) Grade 7 showed that science is always evolving: each answer opens new questions and ideas change as we explore deeper. (3) Investigation brings these together: questions (wonder) become starting points, and observations are used to improve, that is change, our understanding (evolution). (4) The book wants students to learn how to find new facts, not just learn facts, so each becomes an investigator who observes carefully, experiments thoughtfully and explains clearly. (5) Example puzzles: everyday ones such as why dough rises, or bigger mysteries such as whether the world is getting warmer.
s: Grade 6: wonder, simple why and how questions
Grade 7: science evolves, answers open new questions
Investigation uses questions as starting points and observations to improve understanding
Aim: learn how to find new facts; observe, experiment, explain
A puzzle from the chapter: dough rising or the world getting warmer

questions.q:
Rohit's revision notes on two ideas from the book got swapped:
Line 1 (Grade 7): 'Science is always evolving means we design simple experiments to answer focused questions.'
Line 2 (Grade 8): 'Investigation means our answers can change, and each answer opens new questions.'
Rewrite each line correctly, with a puri example for each.
questions.a: Line 1 (Grade 7): science is always evolving: our answers can change as we explore deeper, and each answer opens new questions; e.g. an idea about why a puri puffs may later be replaced by a better one. Line 2 (Grade 8): investigation means asking a focused question and designing a simple experiment, then using the observations; e.g. frying puris in oil at different temperatures and observing whether they puff.
s: Line 1 corrected: answers change and open new questions, with a puri example
Line 2 corrected: focused question plus simple experiment and observation, with a puri example

questions.q:
A student summarises how the Curiosity books have described science across three grades.
Statement 1: In Grade 6, science began with wonder and simple 'Why?' and 'How?' questions.
Statement 2: In Grade 7, the book showed that each answer in science is final and closes the question for good.
Statement 3: In Grade 8, investigation means asking focused questions, designing simple experiments and using observations to improve understanding.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the book's view, a Grade 8 investigation still begins with a question, just as Grade 6 science did.
Reason (R): The book says we learn to use questions as starting points to observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully and explain clearly.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A residential school in Jorhat has 200 students. After the rains, 30 of them fell ill with a stomach infection caused by tiny organisms, and these 30 are being given medicines. The nurse's register shows:
Vaccinated against this infection: 184 students
Skip breakfast on most days: 70 students
Play outdoors less than once a week: 52 students
(a) The nurse says, 'Microbes made these children ill, so we must get rid of every microbe in their bodies.' Use the chapter to explain why this goes too far.
(b) The chapter names four things that help us stay healthy and fight infections. Which of the four does each line of the register (including the medicines) tell us about?
(c) How many students are not vaccinated, and how many more students skip breakfast than are not vaccinated?
(d) The school can afford only one new step this term: a second vaccine camp for the students not yet vaccinated, or a free nutritious breakfast for everyone. Decide which step reaches more students who are missing one of the chapter's ways of staying healthy, using (c).
questions.a: (a) Not all microbes are harmful: the chapter says some are invisible helpers, such as those that help us digest our food, while only others cause infections. Getting rid of every microbe would also remove the helpers. (b) Medicines for the 30 ill students: medicines. Vaccinated line: vaccines. Breakfast line: nutritious food. Outdoor play line: exercise. (c) 200 - 184 = 16 students are not vaccinated; 70 - 16 = 54 more students skip breakfast. (d) The free nutritious breakfast: it reaches the 70 students who miss nutritious food in the morning, while a second vaccine camp would reach only the 16 unvaccinated students.
s: Part (a): some microbes are helpers (digestion), so not all should be removed
Part (b): medicines, vaccines, nutritious food and exercise matched to the register
Part (c): 16 not vaccinated; 54 more skip breakfast
Part (d): breakfast, as it reaches 70 students against 16

questions.q:
Ravi's plan for the month after he recovers from a fever:
Food: instant noodles or chips for dinner on most days
Exercise: none; three hours of mobile games every day
Vaccine: skip the booster due this month, 'since I am not ill now'
Medicines: 'I will keep a strip ready in case I fall ill again'
Evaluate his plan against the chapter's list of what helps us stay healthy and fight infections.
questions.a: The chapter names nutritious food, exercise, medicines and vaccines. Ravi's plan covers only medicines. It falls short on the other three: his dinners are not nutritious, he plans no exercise, and he is skipping a vaccine even though vaccines help us stay healthy. So the plan leaves out three of the four.
s: Judgement: only medicines are covered, so the plan falls short
Names the gaps: nutritious food, exercise and the vaccine

questions.q:
Match each everyday situation in Column I with the idea from the chapter's preview that it shows, in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A pump whose motor spins to push water up to the tank | a. Heating effect of electric current
2. An electric blanket whose wires get warm on a winter night | b. Magnetic effect of electric current
3. A scooter stops when its brakes are applied | c. A force that slows an object down
4. Tiny organisms in our gut help us digest food | d. A microbe that is an invisible helper
At a health camp in Nashik, a nurse gives vaccines to children who are not ill at all. A parent asks why a healthy child needs one. Which reply matches the chapter?
questions.a: Vaccines help us stay healthy as well as fight infections
o: Vaccines help us stay healthy as well as fight infections
Vaccines are needed only by children who already have an infection
Vaccines do the work of nutritious food, so diet stops mattering
Vaccines take the place of exercise for children who are not ill

questions.q: Under a microscope, a drop of water from a village pond shows many tiny moving organisms. Riya says, 'All of these must be harmful, since they are living in pond water.' Which correction fits what the chapter says about such organisms?
questions.a: Some help, as in digestion or making medicines; others cause infections
o: Some help, as in digestion or making medicines; others cause infections
All microbes are helpers, and none of them can ever cause infections
Microbes are not living things, so they cannot harm or help anyone
Microbes live only in dirty water, so they are not linked to our own bodies

questions.q: Write one short everyday situation (one sentence each) for each of the following, so that a classmate could tell which idea it shows: (i) a microbe acting as an invisible helper, (ii) a harmful microbe, (iii) one of the chapter's ways of staying healthy and fighting infection.
questions.a: Example: (i) Tiny organisms living in Meera's gut help her digest her lunch. (ii) A cut on Raju's knee becomes infected by microbes. (iii) Raju's younger sister is given a vaccine at the health centre (or eats nutritious food, exercises, takes medicine).
s: (i) a helper microbe situation (digestion or medicine)
(ii) a harmful microbe causing infection
(iii) nutritious food, exercise, medicine or vaccine used to stay healthy

questions.q: In a kabaddi match, a raider runs in a straight line and then turns sharply at the same speed to dodge a defender. Which statement fits the chapter's description of what forces do?
questions.a: A force acted, because the raider changed direction
o: A force acted, because the raider changed direction
No force acted, because the raider's speed stayed the same
A force acted only while the raider was speeding up
No force acted, because forces only slow things down

questions.q: True or False? 'A cricket ball thrown straight up comes back down because no force acts on it once it leaves the hand.' Give the verdict and the correct idea.
questions.a: False. The chapter says understanding forces explains why a ball thrown up in the air falls back to the ground; a force does act on the ball after it leaves the hand, and that force brings it back down.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a force acts on the ball and brings it back down

questions.q: Under a microscope, Arif finds a kind of tiny organism he has never seen before. Which observation would show that it is a helper rather than a harmful microbe, in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: A factory uses it to make a medicine that treats patients
o: A factory uses it to make a medicine that treats patients
It is far too tiny to be seen without using a microscope
It was found living in a single drop of village pond water
It moves about quickly and is present in very large numbers

questions.q:
(a) The book calls microbes 'unseen but deeply linked to us'. Give one way they are linked to our digestion and one way they are linked to our illnesses.
(b) Why does it make sense for the book to go straight from microbes to the question 'What does our body need to stay healthy?'
questions.a: (a) Some microbes are invisible helpers that help us digest our food; others are harmful and cause infections. (b) Because some microbes cause infections, the next thing to understand is how we stay healthy and fight infections, which the book says nutritious food, exercise, medicines and vaccines help us do.
s: Part (a): helpers in digestion; harmful ones cause infections
Part (b): infections lead to the question of staying healthy, via food, exercise, medicines, vaccines

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After describing how electric current does useful work, the book moves on to study forces.
Reason (R): The book says the heating and magnetic effects of electric current depend on fundamental forces.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Electric current is useful in our homes only because it can make things hot.' Is he right, partly right or wrong? Explain with the chapter's ideas and one example.
questions.a: Partly right. Electric current is useful because of its heating effect, which keeps us warm (e.g. a room heater). But the chapter also describes its magnetic effect, which helps motors run and machines function (e.g. a fan or a water pump), so 'only' is wrong.
s: Verdict: partly right
Heating effect is a real use, with example
Magnetic effect also runs motors and machines, with example

questions.q:
Anika's revision sheet on the first stops of the book's journey has five sentences, each with one mistake in its reasoning. Find the mistake in each and write the corrected idea.
1. 'Microbes must be harmful, because we cannot see them.'
2. 'A ball thrown up comes back down because the push from the hand runs out and no force acts on it any more.'
3. 'A vaccine is a kind of medicine, so a child who is not ill does not need one.'
4. 'A room heater and a ceiling fan both run on electric current, so they both use the same effect of current.'
5. 'The book studies forces right after electricity only because forces are a harder topic.'
questions.a: 1. Being unseen says nothing about harm: some microbes are invisible helpers (they help us digest food or produce medicines) and only some cause infections. 2. A force does act on the ball after it leaves the hand; the book says understanding forces explains why a ball thrown up falls back to the ground. 3. The book lists vaccines along with nutritious food, exercise and medicines as things that help us stay healthy and fight infections, so they are not only for those who are ill. 4. The heater uses the heating effect to keep us warm, while the fan's motor runs on the magnetic effect. 5. The book moves to forces because the effects of electric current depend on fundamental forces.
s: 1. unseen does not mean harmful; some microbes help
2. a force acts on the ball and brings it back
3. vaccines help us stay healthy, not only the ill
4. heater: heating effect; fan motor: magnetic effect
5. the effects of current depend on fundamental forces

questions.q:
Read the three statements about the first stops on the book's journey.
Statement 1: Every microbe found in a drop of water is harmful to us.
Statement 2: When a car stops after its brakes are applied, a force has slowed it down.
Statement 3: It is the heating effect of electric current that makes a motor run.
Which statement or statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
In a Class 8 lesson in Bhopal, the teacher shows three microscope slides, each holding tiny organisms that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
Slide 1: a drop of water from the school tank, full of tiny moving organisms
Slide 2: organisms from a factory tank where they are used to make a medicine
Slide 3: organisms taken from a patient's infected throat
(a) Classify the organisms on Slides 2 and 3 as helpers or harmful, with a reason.
(b) Can the class tell, just from seeing them on Slide 1, whether those organisms are helpers or harmful? Explain using the chapter.
(c) Apart from medicines, name two things the chapter says help us stay healthy and fight infections like the one on Slide 3.
(d) The class can study only one slide's organisms further this week, to find out what they do. Decide which slide they should choose so that they learn something new, using your answers to (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Slide 2: helpers, because they help produce medicines. Slide 3: harmful, because they cause an infection. (b) No. The chapter says some microbes are helpers and some are harmful, so merely seeing that they are present does not show what they do; the class would need to find out what effect they have. (c) Any two of nutritious food, exercise and vaccines. (d) Slide 1. What the organisms on Slides 2 and 3 do is already known (helpers and harmful), but (b) showed that just seeing the Slide 1 organisms does not tell whether they help or harm, so studying them is the only choice that adds new knowledge.
s: Part (a): Slide 2 helpers (medicines); Slide 3 harmful (infection)
Part (b): no; microbes can be helpers or harmful, so presence alone does not tell
Part (c): two of nutritious food, exercise, vaccines
Part (d): Slide 1, since 2 and 3 are already known and Slide 1's effect is unknown

questions.q: In Leela's story, tiny organisms (1) help her digest her lunch, (2) infect a cut on her brother's knee, (3) are used in a factory to produce a medicine, (4) cause her grandfather's throat infection, and (5) give her cousin a stomach infection after he drinks dirty water. Going by the chapter, the number of these five roles in which the microbes act as invisible helpers is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

A hair dryer has a coil that gets hot and a small motor that spins a fan to blow the air out.
(a) Which part uses the heating effect and which uses the magnetic effect of electric current?
(b) One morning the dryer blows only cold air, though the fan spins normally. Which effect has stopped working, and how can you tell?
questions.a: (a) The hot coil uses the heating effect; the motor that spins the fan uses the magnetic effect. (b) The heating effect has stopped (the coil is not heating); the magnetic effect is still working because the motor and fan run.
s: Part (a): coil = heating effect; motor = magnetic effect
Part (b): heating effect has failed, magnetic effect still works

questions.q:
A ceiling fan is switched on. Its blades start from rest and spin faster and faster; when it is switched off, they spin slower and slower and then stop.
(a) Which effect of electric current runs the fan's motor, according to the chapter?
(b) What is a force doing to the blades just after the fan is switched on, and just after it is switched off?
questions.a: (a) The magnetic effect: the chapter says the magnetic effect of electric current helps motors run and machines function. (b) Just after switching on, a force is making the blades speed up; just after switching off, a force is slowing them down.
s: Part (a): magnetic effect runs the motor
Part (b): speeding up after switch-on, slowing down after switch-off

questions.q:
Sameer's cycle computer records his speed every 10 seconds on the way to school in Mysuru.
Time (s) | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70
Speed (km/h) | 0 | 8 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | 6 | 0
The road is straight except between 30 s and 40 s, where it curves round a temple. He brakes for the school gate at the end.
(a) Between which times is a force making the cycle speed up, and by how much does the speed rise?
(b) Between which times is a force slowing it down, and by how much does the speed fall?
(c) Between 30 s and 40 s the speed reading does not change. Does the chapter's description of forces still apply there? Explain.
(d) At the gate his water bottle slips off and falls to the ground. Which example in the chapter is this like, and what does it show?
(e) His friend says, 'The speed row alone shows every stretch where a force changed the motion.' Judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) From 0 s to 20 s; the speed rises by 15 km/h (0 to 15). (b) From 50 s to 70 s; the speed falls by 15 km/h (15 to 0). (c) Yes. The chapter says forces make objects speed up, slow down or change direction; on the curve the cycle changes direction, so a force acts even though the speed stays at 15 km/h. (d) It is like the chapter's ball thrown up that falls back to the ground: a force acts on the bottle and brings it down. (e) The claim is wrong: the speed row misses the curve between 30 s and 40 s, where only the direction changed, and a change of direction also shows a force at work.
s: (a) 0 to 20 s, rise of 15 km/h
(b) 50 to 70 s, fall of 15 km/h
(c) yes: direction changes on the curve, so a force acts
(d) like the ball that falls back; a force brings it down
(e) claim wrong: speeds miss the change of direction on the curve

questions.q: A teacher plans her term in this order: electric current, then forces, then pressure, then winds and cyclones. A student suggests starting with cyclones, 'because they are the most exciting', and doing forces last. Using the links the book draws between these topics, explain why the book's order works better, and give one everyday example of a force that the book mentions.
questions.a: The book says the effects of electric current depend on fundamental forces, so after watching electricity do work it studies forces themselves. Understanding forces leads to pressure, which is how force is distributed over an object, and the same ideas of force and pressure decide how air moves: a small pressure difference gives a gentle breeze and a stronger one strong winds, sometimes cyclones. So cyclones cannot be understood before forces and pressure. Example: a ball thrown up falls back to the ground, or a car stops when the brakes are applied.
s: Link: effects of current depend on fundamental forces
Chain: forces lead to pressure, which decides how air moves into winds and cyclones
Example: ball falling back or car stopping on braking

questions.q: A student's chart lists: 'Substance K: a compound made of only one element, iron.' Using the chapter's definitions, show that this description cannot be correct, and write what K must actually be.
questions.a: A compound is made of two or more elements bonded together, so a substance made of only one element cannot be a compound. A substance made of iron alone is an element (a pure substance). So K is an element, not a compound.
s: Compound needs two or more elements
One element only, so it cannot be a compound
K is an element

questions.q: Asha sees agarbatti smoke spread across the whole room while a steel spoon on the table keeps its shape all day. She concludes, 'Only the smoke is made of particles; the spoon is one solid piece with no particles in it.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: Both are made of particles; the spoon's particles cannot move much
o: Both are made of particles; the spoon's particles cannot move much
Neither is made of particles; smoke spreads only because it is light
The spoon has particles, but they move around as freely as a gas's
Only solids are made of particles, so the smoke must have none at all

questions.q: On the same afternoon, neighbouring towns M and N both read 1030 hPa, while neighbouring towns S and T read 1004 hPa and 1012 hPa. Going by the chapter, between which pair of towns is a stronger wind more likely?
questions.a: Between S and T, as their pressure difference is larger
o: Between S and T, as their pressure difference is larger
Between M and N, as both of their pressures are high
Between M and N, as equal pressures push air the hardest
Equal at both, as only the average pressure matters

questions.q: True or False? 'A closed, empty-looking room holds nothing at all, because no particles can be seen in it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says everything around us is made of tiny particles. The room is full of air, a gas, whose particles move around freely; not being able to see them does not mean they are absent.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: everything is made of tiny particles; the air in the room is a gas whose particles move freely

questions.q:
Consider these statements from the chapter's preview of pressure and particles.
Statement 1: Pressure is about how a force is distributed over an object.
Statement 2: A stronger pressure difference between places can lead to strong winds and sometimes cyclones.
Statement 3: In a solid, the particles move around freely, just as they do in a gas.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Odd one out: (i) a wire made of copper alone, (ii) a rod made of iron alone, (iii) water, in which hydrogen and oxygen are bonded together, (iv) a foil made of aluminium alone.
(a) Which is the odd one out, and to which of the chapter's classes does it belong?
(b) What single fact from the chapter's definitions separates it from the other three?
questions.a: (a) Water is the odd one out: it is a compound, while copper, iron and aluminium here are each a single pure substance (element). (b) In water two different elements are bonded together, which is what makes a compound; each of the others is made of one element only.
s: Part (a): water, a compound; the rest are elements
Part (b): two or more elements bonded together versus one element only

questions.q:
A lab card describes three materials.
P: made of only one element, copper.
Q: formed when hydrogen and oxygen are bonded together.
R: iron filings stirred into sand, which a magnet can pull apart.
Using the chapter's three classes, which classification is correct?
questions.a: P element, Q compound, R mixture
o: P element, Q compound, R mixture
P element, Q mixture, R compound
P compound, Q element, R mixture
P mixture, Q compound, R element

questions.q: A label on a jar of white powder says: 'Contains three different elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. No physical method such as sieving, a magnet or picking by hand can separate them.' Using the chapter's three classes of materials, the powder is a(n) ___.
questions.a: compound

questions.q:
Compare a solid and a gas in terms of how their particles move, as the chapter describes, and then use the comparison to analyse each observation:
(i) An ice cube kept on a plate keeps its shape for a few minutes.
(ii) Perfume sprayed in one corner of a room is soon smelt in the far corner.
(iii) Air pumped into a flat football spreads into every part of it.
Finally, say which part of the book's journey these ideas will later help explain.
questions.a: Comparison: everything is made of tiny particles; in a solid the particles cannot move much, while in a gas they move around freely. (i) Ice is a solid; its particles cannot move much, so it keeps its shape. (ii) The perfume vapour is a gas; its particles move around freely and spread across the room. (iii) Air is a gas; its particles move freely and spread through the whole football. These ideas later help explain how air exerts pressure and why water boils at a certain temperature.
s: Comparison of particle movement in solids and gases
(i) solid particles cannot move much
(ii) gas particles move freely and spread
(iii) gas spreads to fill the football
Later use: air pressure or water boiling at a certain temperature

questions.q:
Priyanka's lab record for a classification activity reads:
Row | Material | What we know | Her class | Her reason
1 | Copper wire | made of copper alone | element | one pure substance
2 | Water | hydrogen and oxygen bonded together | mixture | it has two elements in it
3 | Sand and iron filings | a magnet pulls the filings out | mixture | separated physically
4 | Common salt | sodium and chlorine bonded together | element | it is a pure substance
5 | Dal and small stones | picked apart by hand | mixture | separated physically
(a) Which two rows contain an error?
(b) Correct each of those rows, giving the right class and reason.
(c) The teacher has five minutes and no magnet for one demonstration that shows what makes a mixture different from a compound. Decide which row's material she should use and what the class will see, using (b).
questions.a: (a) Rows 2 and 4. (b) Row 2: water is a compound, because two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, are bonded together; having two elements does not make it a mixture. Row 4: salt is a compound, because sodium and chlorine are bonded together; it is not an element. (c) Row 5: picking the stones out of the dal by hand shows that a mixture can be separated physically, and it needs no magnet, unlike row 3. Water and salt cannot be pulled apart like this, because in a compound the elements are bonded together.
s: Part (a): rows 2 and 4
Part (b): both are compounds, with elements bonded together
Part (c): row 5, separated by hand without a magnet, unlike the bonded compounds

questions.q:
A teacher prepares four samples and describes each one.
(i) A wire in which every particle is copper.
(ii) Iron filings and sulphur powder ground together; a magnet pulls the iron filings out again.
(iii) The same iron and sulphur after strong heating: they are now bonded together as a new black solid, and the magnet pulls nothing out.
(iv) A jar of gas made of one element only, oxygen.
Classify (i) to (iv) as element, compound or mixture, giving the reason from the chapter's definitions. Then judge Ravi's claim: '(ii) and (iii) must be the same class, because they contain the same two elements.'
questions.a: (i) Element: a pure substance made of copper alone. (ii) Mixture: the iron and sulphur can be separated physically with a magnet. (iii) Compound: the two elements are now bonded together and can no longer be pulled apart by the magnet. (iv) Element: a gas can also be a pure substance made of one element only. Ravi is wrong: the class depends on whether the elements are bonded together or only combined in a way that can be separated physically, not just on which elements are present; (ii) is a mixture and (iii) a compound.
s: (i) element, one element only
(ii) mixture, separated by a magnet
(iii) compound, elements bonded together
(iv) element, a gas of one element
Ravi wrong: bonded or not decides the class, not which elements are present

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To understand why water boils at a certain temperature, the book says we need to zoom into the particles that water is made up of and how they move.
Reason (R): Mixtures are combinations that can be separated physically.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Ananya stirs two spoons of sugar into a cup of hot tea. After a minute she can no longer see any sugar. Which observation best shows that the sugar is still in the cup?
questions.a: Every sip of the tea now tastes sweet
o: Every sip of the tea now tastes sweet
The level of the tea looks the same as before
No sugar crystals can be seen at the bottom
The tea still looks the same brown colour

questions.q: Farhan says, 'Rice grains mixed with small stones are two materials together in one bowl, but they still do not form a compound.' Tara replies, 'Any two materials put together make a compound.' Is Farhan right? Explain using the chapter's classes.
questions.a: Yes, Farhan is right. A compound forms only when two or more elements are bonded together. The rice and stones are only combined and can be separated physically, for example by picking the stones out by hand, so they form a mixture, not a compound. Tara's rule is wrong: putting materials together does not by itself bond them.
s: Verdict: Farhan is right
Compound needs elements bonded together
Rice and stones can be separated physically, so they are a mixture

questions.q:
A weather club records the air pressure (in hPa) at noon in two coastal towns, A and B, which are 100 km apart.
Day | Town A | Town B
Monday | 1008 | 1006
Tuesday | 1010 | 1003
Wednesday | 1012 | 996
Thursday | 1009 | 1008
(a) Work out the pressure difference between the towns on each day.
(b) Using the chapter's idea about pressure differences, arrange the four days from the one most likely to have the gentlest wind to the one most likely to have the strongest wind.
(c) On Friday the difference was 3 hPa more than on Monday, and Town A read 1007 hPa, higher than Town B. What did Town B read?
(d) The school beach picnic can be held only on Tuesday, Wednesday or Friday. Decide the safest of these days for the picnic, using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) Monday 2 hPa, Tuesday 7 hPa, Wednesday 16 hPa, Thursday 1 hPa. (b) Thursday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday: a small pressure difference gives a gentle breeze, a stronger difference gives strong winds and sometimes cyclones. (c) Friday's difference = 2 + 3 = 5 hPa, so Town B read 1007 - 5 = 1002 hPa. (d) Friday: its difference of 5 hPa is smaller than Tuesday's 7 hPa and Wednesday's 16 hPa, so it is least likely to bring strong winds; Wednesday, with the largest difference, is the worst choice.
s: Part (a): differences 2, 7, 16 and 1 hPa
Part (b): order Thursday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, with the pressure-difference reason
Part (c): 5 hPa difference, Town B = 1002 hPa
Part (d): Friday, as its 5 hPa difference is the smallest of the allowed days

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the idea from the chapter that it shows, in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A wire made of copper alone | a. A pure substance (element)
2. Water, with hydrogen and oxygen bonded together | b. Two or more elements bonded together (compound)
3. Sawdust and sand, separated by sieving | c. A combination that can be separated physically (mixture)
4. The smell of agarbatti reaching the far corner of a room | d. Particles of a gas move around freely
In the book's journey, particles and the classification of materials come before solutions. Using the chapter, explain why this order makes sense, with its sugar-and-tea example.
questions.a: The chapter says that once we know how particles combine or mix, we can understand solutions. A solution such as sugar dissolving in tea to make it sweet is about how the particles of sugar and tea mix, so particles and mixing must be understood first.
s: Solutions are understood once we know how particles combine or mix
Sugar dissolving in tea used to show this

questions.q:
A balloon is blown up with air and tied.
(a) Compare how the particles of the air inside and the particles of the rubber skin move, using the chapter.
(b) Why, then, does the air spread to fill every part of the balloon while the rubber does not flow anywhere on its own?
questions.a: (a) The air is a gas, so its particles move around freely; the rubber is a solid, so its particles cannot move much. (b) Because gas particles move around freely, the air spreads out into all of the space inside; the solid rubber's particles cannot move much, so it keeps its own form.
s: Part (a): gas particles move freely; solid particles cannot move much
Part (b): free movement lets the air spread to fill the balloon; the solid keeps its form

questions.q:
(a) Mr Behera, a farmer near Puri, hears two forecasts: Day 1, 'small pressure difference'; Day 2, 'large pressure difference'. Say what kind of wind each day is likely to bring.
(b) Name two areas of life the chapter says such winds can affect, and say which forecast day should worry Mr Behera more.
questions.a: (a) Day 1: a gentle breeze. Day 2: strong winds, and sometimes even a cyclone. (b) The chapter says such winds affect daily life, agriculture and safety (any two). He should worry more about Day 2, as strong winds or a cyclone could harm his crops and his safety.
s: Part (a): small difference = gentle breeze; large difference = strong winds or cyclone
Part (b): two of daily life, agriculture, safety; Day 2 is the worry

questions.q: Write one everyday material or situation that fits each description, and say how it fits: (i) something made of particles that move around freely; (ii) a combination that can be separated physically, with the way you would separate it; (iii) a material in which two or more elements are bonded together, naming the elements.
questions.a: Example: (i) the smell of cooking spreading through a house: the smell travels through air, a gas whose particles move around freely. (ii) Peanuts mixed with puffed rice: picked apart by hand, so it is a mixture. (iii) Water: hydrogen and oxygen are bonded together, so it is a compound (or common salt: sodium and chlorine bonded together).
s: (i) a gas example, with particles moving freely
(ii) a mixture with a physical way of separating it
(iii) a compound with the elements named as bonded

questions.q:
A Class 8 group surveys a village pond in Kutch and records what each living being there needs.
Living being | What it needs
Lotus | water, sunlight
Fish | water, small water plants
Heron | fish, air
Grass on the bank | sunlight, water
Last May the pond shrank to a puddle and many fish died. For this summer the panchayat has two plans. Plan 1: stretch a shade net over half of the pond to cut the water lost to evaporation, leaving the other half open to the sky. Plan 2: leave the pond uncovered, as it is.
(a) Which non-living things in the table are needed by more than one living being?
(b) If all the fish died, which living being in the table would be affected directly, and why?
(c) Decide which plan is better for the pond as an ecosystem. Use the table, your answers to (a) and (b), and the chapter's idea of what living beings depend on.
questions.a: (a) Water (lotus, fish, grass) and sunlight (lotus, grass). (b) The heron, because it needs fish. (c) Plan 1. Water is needed by the lotus, the fish and the grass, and through the fish by the heron, so if the pond dries up again as it did last May, every living being in the table loses out. The half net saves water while the open half still lets sunlight reach the lotus, and the grass on the bank is not under the net at all. Plan 2 keeps full sunlight but risks the water that all of them depend on. The chapter says living beings depend on air, water, sunlight and other organisms, so keeping the water while still letting in sunlight is the better balance.
s: Part (a): water and sunlight
Part (b): heron, as it feeds on fish
Part (c): Plan 1; water loss would hit every living being, while the open half still gives the lotus sunlight

questions.q:
Read these statements about the later stops of the book's journey.
Statement 1: Not only polished mirrors but rough surfaces also reflect light.
Statement 2: Watching the periodic cycles of the Moon's phases helped humans come up with the first calendars.
Statement 3: Earth's atmosphere provides the oxygen we breathe and shields us from harmful ultraviolet rays.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q: From the same rooftop in Jaipur, Aditi sketches the Moon every night for a week and finds a different part of it lit each night. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: Earth, Moon and Sun change positions, so another part is lit
o: Earth, Moon and Sun change positions, so another part is lit
The Moon makes more of its own light on some nights than on others
Clouds cover a different part of the Moon each night of the week
The Moon really changes its actual shape a little every single night

questions.q: The chapter says light reflects off flat and curved mirrors and bends when it passes through lenses. Which of these everyday objects helps a person mainly by bending light?
questions.a: A pair of corrective glasses for reading
o: A pair of corrective glasses for reading
A flat mirror on a dressing table
A curved mirror at a sharp hill-road bend
A polished steel plate used as a mirror

questions.q:
A science magazine describes three imaginary planets.
Planet | Distance from its star | Atmosphere
K | so close that water boils away | no oxygen; blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
L | water stays liquid | no oxygen; lets harmful ultraviolet rays through
M | water stays liquid | rich in oxygen; lets harmful ultraviolet rays through
Check each planet against the conditions the chapter gives for Earth being 'just right' for life, decide which planet comes closest, say what it still lacks, and name one way the chapter says Earth's own balance can be disturbed.
questions.a: The chapter's conditions: lying at the distance where water remains liquid, an atmosphere that provides oxygen, and an atmosphere that shields living beings from harmful ultraviolet rays. K: fails distance and oxygen; meets the ultraviolet shield (1 of 3). L: meets distance; fails oxygen and the shield (1 of 3). M: meets distance and oxygen; fails the shield (2 of 3). M comes closest, but it still lacks a shield against harmful ultraviolet rays, so it is not 'just right' for life like ours. Earth's balance: human activities can cause small changes in Earth's temperature, disrupting climate patterns with dangerous consequences.
s: K checked: fails distance and oxygen, has the UV shield
L checked: liquid water only, fails oxygen and shield
M checked: water and oxygen, no UV shield
Judgement: M closest but lacks the UV shield
Human activities cause small temperature changes that disrupt climate

questions.q:
In a paddy-growing village in Kerala, a strong spray wipes out the frogs in the fields. Over the next season, the farmers find far more insects eating their crop.
(a) Which part of the chapter's description of ecosystems does this show?
(b) Predict one more living being in the fields that could be affected, and say through which link.
questions.a: (a) Every living being depends on and responds to the air, water, sunlight and other organisms around it: frogs and insects are linked, so losing the frogs changed the insects, and that changed the crop. (b) For example, birds or snakes that eat frogs would have less food; or the paddy plants suffer because more insects feed on them.
s: Part (a): living beings depend on and respond to other organisms
Part (b): another affected living being with its link

questions.q: Kiran says, 'The Moon is not a polished mirror, yet it reflects light, just as a rough wall does. A different part of it looks lit each night because the Earth, Moon and Sun keep changing their positions relative to one another.' Her friend says a surface that is not shiny cannot reflect light. Is Kiran right? Support your answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, Kiran is right. The chapter says it is not just a polished mirror that reflects light; rough surfaces reflect light as well, and so does the Moon. It also says that, depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is illuminated each night, which gives its phases. Her friend is wrong.
s: Verdict: Kiran is right
Rough surfaces and the Moon also reflect light
Relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun decide the lit part

questions.q: A heritage club in Ujjain wants to rebuild an old-style calendar using only what can be seen in the sky. Which plan uses the observations the chapter says calendars came from?
questions.a: Record sunrises, sunsets and the Moon's phases night after night
o: Record sunrises, sunsets and the Moon's phases night after night
Measure how far away the Moon is from the Earth on every night
Count all the stars that can be seen on one clear and dark night
Sketch the Moon carefully on one single night and copy its shape

questions.q:
(a) In Lakshmi's village, a month runs from one purnima to the next. Which pattern in the sky is this month built on?
(b) The chapter calls it fascinating that the calendars which set our routines are linked to objects far beyond our planet. Explain this link with the village month.
questions.a: (a) The periodic cycle of the Moon's phases: the full Moon returns at the end of each cycle. (b) The village fixes its months, and so its routines, by watching the Moon, an object far beyond Earth. The chapter says watching these periodic cycles let humans make the first calendars, and combining them with sunrises and sunsets gave various calendars.
s: Part (a): the periodic cycle of the Moon's phases
Part (b): routines on Earth are set by watching the Moon, as the first calendars were

questions.q: A science-fiction story describes a planet where water stays liquid and the air has oxygen, but nothing in its air stops harmful ultraviolet rays. Of the chapter's three conditions that make Earth 'just right' for life, the number this planet meets is ___. (Write the number in digits.)
True or False? 'A rough, white-washed wall reflects light, even though we cannot see our face in it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says it is not just a polished mirror that reflects light; rough surfaces reflect light as well (and so does the Moon). Not seeing a clear image does not mean no light is reflected.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rough surfaces also reflect light, as the chapter says

questions.q:
A school eco-club in Chennai wants to find out whether their town is getting warmer.
(a) One member says, 'We can just ask our grandparents whether summers feel hotter now.' Which of the habits the chapter calls key for protecting Earth's balance does this plan lack?
(b) Plan one measurement the club could make, saying where, when and how often.
questions.a: (a) It relies on memory and feeling, so it lacks measuring; the chapter names observing, measuring and experimenting as the key habits. (b) For example: read a thermometer kept in the same shaded spot at the same time, say 2 p.m., every day, and compare the monthly averages from one year to the next.
s: Part (a): lacks measuring (observing, measuring, experimenting are key)
Part (b): a repeated measurement with place, time and frequency

questions.q: A long drought dries up a village pond in Bundelkhand. Which conclusion best fits the chapter's description of ecosystems?
questions.a: Fish, water plants, frogs and herons will all suffer
o: Fish, water plants, frogs and herons will all suffer
Only the fish, as only they live inside the water
Only the fish and the herons, but not the water plants
Only the water plants, as animals can move to another pond

questions.q: Deepa says, 'Human activities cause only small changes in Earth's temperature, so they cannot really harm the planet.' Is she right? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says human activities can cause small changes in the temperature of the Earth, but even these small changes disrupt climate patterns with dangerous consequences. So 'small' does not mean harmless.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Human activity does cause small temperature changes
Even small changes disrupt climate patterns, with dangerous consequences

questions.q: Astronomers describe a planet so close to its star that any water on it would boil away. Its atmosphere has oxygen and blocks harmful ultraviolet rays. Which of the chapter's 'just right' conditions for Earth does this planet fail?
questions.a: Lying at the distance where water stays liquid
o: Lying at the distance where water stays liquid
Having an atmosphere that gives oxygen to breathe
Having an atmosphere that shields from ultraviolet rays
Being close enough to its star to receive sunlight

questions.q:
Match each everyday experience in Column I with the idea from the chapter that explains it, in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Corrective glasses help Dadi read the newspaper | a. Light reflecting off a flat mirror
2. Ravi sees himself in the bathroom mirror | b. Light bending as it passes through lenses
3. Why a different part of the Moon is lit on different nights | c. Periodic cycles of the Moon's phases
4. Early humans made the first calendars | d. Changing positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun

(a) Light falls on Ravi's dressing-table mirror and on Dadi's reading glasses. What does the light do at each, according to the chapter?
(b) Dadi says her glasses help her see 'because they work like a small mirror in front of my eyes'. Correct her.
questions.a: (a) At the mirror, light reflects off the surface; at the glasses, which are lenses, light bends as it passes through. (b) Her glasses are lenses, not mirrors: light passes through them and bends, and the chapter says this bending of light explains how corrective glasses help many of us see clearly.
s: Part (a): mirror reflects light; lens bends light passing through
Part (b): glasses are lenses that bend light, not mirrors

questions.q: Write a short situation (one or two sentences) for each of these, set in an Indian town: (i) people as part of the problem of Earth's changing climate, as the chapter describes it; (ii) people using science to understand the change and guide their actions. Then (iii) explain how your two situations show the chapter's line that 'at the heart of both the problem and any possible solution is us'.
questions.a: Example: (i) The everyday activities of a growing town's people add to the small changes in Earth's temperature that the chapter says can disrupt climate patterns. (ii) A school group records the town's temperature every day for ten years and uses the record to guide what the town decides to do. (iii) Both situations are about people: in (i) human activity causes the change, and in (ii) humans use science to understand it and guide action, so 'us' is at the heart of both.
s: (i) a situation where human activity changes Earth's temperature or climate
(ii) a situation where science is used to understand and guide action
(iii) humans are behind both the problem and the solution

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Earth's atmosphere helps life by shielding living beings from harmful ultraviolet rays.
Reason (R): The atmosphere is what keeps Earth at the right distance from the Sun for water to remain liquid.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Lakshmi, who lives in a village in Telangana, keeps a Moon diary, counting the night of purnima as Night 1.
Night | What she saw
1 | Full Moon, fully bright
8 | About half of the Moon bright
15 | Moon not seen at all
23 | About half of the Moon bright
30 | Full Moon again
(a) Lakshmi missed Night 4. Was the bright part on Night 4 larger or smaller than on Night 8? Give the reason from her diary and the chapter.
(b) Using the chapter, explain why a different part of the Moon looks bright on different nights.
(c) How many nights after the first purnima did the next purnima come?
(d) The village wants to hold its monthly fair on the brightest night of each cycle, as the fairground has no electric lights. On which night number, counting on from Night 1, should the fair after Night 30 be held? Justify using (c).
questions.a: (a) Larger. The diary shows the bright part shrinking from full on Night 1 to half on Night 8 and none on Night 15, and the chapter's last page also speaks of the bright part of the Moon shrinking after purnima; Night 4 comes before Night 8 in this shrinking stretch, so more of the Moon was lit. (b) Depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is illuminated each night. (c) 30 - 1 = 29 nights. (d) Night 59. The phases repeat in a periodic cycle, and the diary shows purnima returning after 29 nights, so the next full Moon is expected 29 nights after Night 30: 30 + 29 = 59.
s: Part (a): larger on Night 4, as the bright part shrinks after purnima
Part (b): relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun
Part (c): 29 nights
Part (d): Night 59, using the repeating 29-night cycle

questions.q: Compare and analyse how three things deal with light: a flat bathroom mirror, a rough mud wall, and the Moon. Then use your comparison to explain (i) why we see the Moon at night at all and (ii) why the lit part of the Moon looks different on different nights, and (iii) how this helped humans long ago.
questions.a: Comparison: the flat mirror reflects light (we see a clear image); the rough wall also reflects light, though we see no clear image; the Moon also reflects light. (i) We see the Moon because it reflects light that falls on it. (ii) Depending on the relative positions of the Earth, Moon and Sun, a slightly different part of the Moon is lit each night, giving its phases. (iii) Watching these periodic cycles allowed humans to make the first calendars.
s: Mirror reflects light
Rough wall and Moon also reflect light
(i) Moon is seen because it reflects light
(ii) relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun change the lit part
(iii) periodic phases led to the first calendars

questions.q:
(a) Rewrite the wondering question 'Why does a batura puff up so much?' as a scientific question in the same form as the chapter's question about puris.
(b) Name two things you could control to answer your question in (a).
questions.a: (a) 'What are the different things that may change the way a batura puffs up when fried?' (b) Any two of: the thickness or size of the rolled dough, the type of flour, the temperature of the oil, the way the dough is put into the oil.
s: Part (a): question about what things may change how a batura puffs
Part (b): two controllable things

questions.q:
Kavya moves the chapter's way of planning from puris to melting ice. Her question: 'What are the different things that may change how fast an ice cube melts?'
(a) Name two things she could change or control.
(b) Name one thing she could observe or measure to see whether her changes made a difference.
questions.a: (a) For example: the size of the ice cube, where it is kept (in the sun or in the shade), or whether it sits on a steel or a plastic plate. (b) For example: the time in minutes until it melts completely, or whether it has fully melted after 10 minutes.
s: Part (a): two things she can change or control
Part (b): one observation or measurement of melting

questions.q: Kunal's plan reads: 'Controlled: whether the puri puffs up. Observed: the type of flour.' Show that this plan cannot work as written, and rewrite it correctly.
questions.a: He cannot decide beforehand whether a puri will puff; that is a result we watch for, so it cannot be 'controlled'. The type of flour is chosen by us before frying, so it is not something we observe. Correct plan: Controlled: the type of flour (atta or maida). Observed: whether the puri puffs up.
s: Puffing is a result, so it cannot be controlled
Flour type is chosen, so it is not an observation
Correct swap: control flour type; observe puffing

questions.q: Four friends each write a question about puris. Which question is closest to the chapter's idea of a scientific question, one you can answer by changing something and observing what happens?
questions.a: Does the dough's thickness change how a puri puffs?
o: Does the dough's thickness change how a puri puffs?
Why do so many families make puris only on festival days?
Who was the very first person to fry a puri in India?
Are puris tastier than chapatis for most people we know?

questions.q:
Three statements about starting a scientific investigation, as in the chapter.
Statement 1: You need a proper, well-equipped laboratory before you can do any scientific experiment.
Statement 2: The type of flour, atta or maida, is one of the things we can control in the puri investigation.
Statement 3: Before experimenting, we try to find both what we can change or control and what we can observe.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Each change in Column I was made in a puri experiment. Match it with the controllable thing in Column II that it changes.
Column I | Column II
1. One circle rolled to 2 mm, another to 4 mm | a. Thickness of the rolled dough
2. One batch made with maida, one with atta | b. Type of flour
3. Dough slid in at an angle instead of dropped straight down | c. Temperature of the oil
4. Oil heated until it just shimmers, then heated until it is boiling hot | d. Way the dough is put into the oil

Compare two questions from Class 8 students.
Q1: 'Why is one side of a puri thinner than the other?'
Q2: 'Does dropping the dough vertically or sliding it in at an angle change whether one side turns out thinner?'
(a) Which question is set up so that a simple experiment can answer it? Explain.
(b) For that question, state what is controlled and what is observed.
(c) Is Q1 then useless? Justify your view using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Q2. It names one thing we can change (the way the dough goes into the oil) and one result we can see (whether one side is thinner), so a simple experiment can answer it. Q1 asks 'why' without saying what to change or watch. (b) Controlled: the way the dough is put into the oil (vertical or at an angle). Observed: whether one side of the puri turns out thinner. (c) No. Q1 is the curious question the chapter itself starts from, and scientific questions like Q2 grow out of such curiosity. The chapter also says even the puffing of a puri is not completely understood by scientists today, so such questions are worth asking.
s: (a) Q2 can be tested
(a) reason: names a change and a result, Q1 does not
(b) controlled: way of dropping; observed: thinner side
(c) Q1 is not useless: it is the starting curiosity
(c) the chapter says even puri puffing is not completely understood, so such questions are worth asking

questions.q: Gauri wants to carry the chapter's puri plan over to a phulka swelling on a direct flame. Which item from the chapter's list of things we can control while frying a puri can she NOT use as it is?
questions.a: The temperature of the hot oil
o: The temperature of the hot oil
The thickness of the rolled dough
The size of the rolled dough circle
The type of flour, atta or maida

questions.q: While frying baturas, Simran changes only one thing: she slides the dough in slowly at an angle instead of dropping it straight down. Which of the chapter's controllable things has she changed?
questions.a: The way the dough is put into the oil
o: The way the dough is put into the oil
The thickness and size of the rolled dough
The type of flour used to make the dough
The temperature of the oil in the kadhai

questions.q: Rehana lists things for her puri investigation. Which one is something she will observe, not something she controls?
questions.a: Whether the puri puffs up in the oil
o: Whether the puri puffs up in the oil
The thickness of the rolled-out dough
The type of flour, atta or maida
The temperature of the hot oil

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the puri investigation, the temperature of the oil is something we observe rather than something we control.
Reason (R): The chapter lists changing the temperature of the hot oil among the things we can do while frying.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Arnav writes his plan: 'I will test atta and maida puris.' Nothing else is written. The chapter says we must find two main things before experimenting. Which of the two has Arnav found, which has he left out, and give one example of what he could add.
questions.a: He has found what he will change or control: the type of flour. He has left out what he will observe to see whether the change made a difference. He could add, for example, 'whether each puri puffs up' or 'the time each takes to puff, in seconds'.
s: Found: what he controls (flour type)
Missing: what he will observe, with an example

questions.q: Mehul says, 'In the puri investigation, the type of flour counts as something I can control, but the way the dough goes into the oil does not, because it is over in a second.' Is he right, partly right or wrong? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the type of flour (atta, maida) is something we can control. He is wrong about the way the dough goes in: the chapter lists dropping it vertically, sliding it at an angle or sliding it slowly among the things we can control, however quickly it happens.
s: Verdict: partly right
Flour type is something we control
The way the dough is put in is also listed as controllable

questions.q: Tanu wants to test every way of putting the dough into the oil that the chapter suggests, each one different, frying 4 puris for each way. The number of dough circles she must roll is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

Class 8B in Amritsar has one kadhai, a stopwatch, atta dough and 40 minutes for one investigation. Four groups propose:
Group | Question | Settings tried | Puris needed | Minutes needed
P | Does oil temperature change the time to puff? | 3 oil temperatures | 9 | 45
Q | Does the size of the circle change whether it puffs? | 2 sizes | 6 | 20
R | Why is one side of a puri thinner than the other? | none named | none | not known
S | Does the way the dough goes in change whether one side is thinner? | 3 ways | 9 | 25
(a) Which proposal is not yet set up as a question an experiment can answer, and what is missing from it?
(b) Group Q records only whether each puri puffs. Suggest an observation with a number that would suit its question, and say why it helps.
(c) Which proposals can be finished in the 40 minutes?
(d) The class wants the one plan that fits in 40 minutes and tries the most different settings of the thing it changes. Decide which plan to run.
questions.a: (a) R: it asks 'why' but names nothing to change or control and nothing to observe, so no experiment is set up yet. (b) The time each puri takes to puff, in seconds; a number shows how much faster one size puffs, not just whether it puffs. (c) Q (20 minutes) and S (25 minutes); P needs 45 minutes, more than the 40 available, and Q and S together would need 45 minutes as well. (d) S: it fits in 25 minutes and tries 3 settings (three ways of putting the dough in), while Q tries only 2 sizes.
s: Part (a): R, nothing to change or observe is named
Part (b): time to puff in seconds, which allows exact comparison
Part (c): Q and S fit; P needs 45 minutes
Part (d): S, 3 settings within 25 minutes against Q's 2

questions.q: A student's record says: 'Changed: the way the dough went into the oil (dropped vertically, slid at an angle, slid slowly). Watched: whether one side of the puri came out thinner.' Write the scientific question she was trying to answer, and name two other things she could control that she should leave unchanged.
questions.a: Question: 'Does the way the dough is put into the oil change whether one side of the puri comes out thinner?' Two other controllable things: any two of the thickness of the dough, the size of the dough circle, the type of flour, the temperature of the oil.
s: A question linking the way of dropping to the thinner side
First other controllable thing
Second other controllable thing

questions.q:
Tara and her brother want to do one kitchen investigation this weekend. At home they have atta (but no maida), one kadhai, oil, a rolling pin and a stopwatch. They shortlist three questions.
Q-A: Does atta or maida make a puri puff better?
Q-B: Does the thickness of the rolled dough change how quickly a puri puffs?
Q-C: Why do puris taste better at weddings?
(a) Decide which question they can actually investigate this weekend, and give one reason.
(b) For your chosen question, state what they will change and what they will observe.
(c) Tara also wants to check the chapter's question 'Does a very thick layer of dough still give a thin side?' In that check, what is she controlling and what is she observing?
(d) Rewrite Q-C as a question about frying puris that could be tested by changing one thing and observing the result.
questions.a: (a) Q-B: they have everything needed (dough, oil, rolling pin, stopwatch), and it asks about something they can change and observe. (b) Change: the thickness of the rolled dough. Observe: how quickly the puri puffs (time in seconds) or whether it puffs. (c) She controls the thickness of the dough (she rolls a very thick layer on purpose); she observes whether one side of the puri still comes out thin. (d) Example: 'Does the temperature of the oil change how well a puri puffs?' or 'Does sliding the dough in slowly instead of dropping it change how it puffs?'
s: Part (a): Q-B, materials available and testable
Part (b): changes thickness; observes puffing or time to puff
Part (c): controls thickness (a very thick layer); observes whether a thin side still forms
Part (d): a testable question with one thing to change and a result to observe

questions.q:
Your class will investigate the question: 'Does the size of the dough circle change how quickly a puri puffs?'
(a) State exactly how you will change the size.
(b) Name the other things from the chapter's list of things we can control, and give the fixed setting you will use for each.
(c) State what you will observe or measure, and how you will record it.
(d) Explain why every item in (b) must stay the same in all the trials.
questions.a: (a) For example: roll circles of three sizes, 8 cm, 10 cm and 12 cm across, with three puris of each size. (b) Thickness: every circle rolled to the same thickness, say 3 mm; flour: all atta from one dough; oil temperature: the same hot oil for every puri; way of putting in: every circle slid in at an angle in the same way. (c) The time in seconds from entering the oil until it puffs, measured with a stopwatch and written in a table for each size (also whether it puffs at all). (d) The chapter says it is better to change only one thing at a time while keeping the other conditions the same; if the thickness also changed, for example, we could not tell whether the size or the thickness caused a difference in time.
s: (a) a clear plan for changing the size
(b) thickness, flour, oil temperature and way of putting in, each with a fixed setting
(c) a measured or yes/no observation and how it is recorded
(d) change one thing at a time so the cause can be told

questions.q: True or False? 'In the puri investigation, the time a puri takes to puff up is one of the things we control.' Give the verdict and the correct idea.
