questions.a: False. The time taken to puff up is something we observe or measure (in seconds), as a result of the changes. The things we control include the thickness and size of the dough, the type of flour, the oil temperature and the way the dough is dropped in.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: time to puff is observed or measured, not controlled

questions.q:
Mitali says, 'We have no science lab at home, so I cannot do any experiments in the holidays.'
(a) Is she right? Answer using what the chapter says you need to start.
(b) Write one 'what happens if...?' question she could test in her kitchen with a batura or a phulka.
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter says you don't need a fancy laboratory; even the kitchen at home is a wonderful place to observe and ask questions, and all you need is curiosity, careful observation and asking 'what happens if...?'. (b) For example: 'What happens if I roll the phulka thinner before putting it on the flame: does it swell faster?'
s: Part (a): not right; the kitchen is enough, with curiosity, careful observation and 'what happens if'
Part (b): a testable 'what happens if' question about a batura or phulka

questions.q: Nikhil is testing whether flour type changes how a puri puffs. Midway, the oil starts to smoke, but he does not write it down because 'it was not part of my question'. Which piece of the chapter's advice has he skipped?
questions.a: Keep notes of everything you see and sense
o: Keep notes of everything you see and sense
Change only one thing at a time in a trial
Measure the puffing time in exact seconds
Use dough circles of exactly the same size

questions.q: Two groups compare three oil temperatures. Group A writes 'puffed: yes' for every puri; Group B times every puri with a stopwatch. Which group can tell which oil made the puris puff fastest?
questions.a: Group B, as times in seconds show how much faster each was
o: Group B, as times in seconds show how much faster each was
Group A, as a yes or no answer is more certain than a time
Both equally, as any observation shows how fast it puffed
Neither, as the speed of puffing cannot ever be observed

questions.q: Rahul says, 'My first round of puri trials raised three new questions that I cannot answer yet, so my experiment has failed.' Is he right? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that after doing one round of experiments you may think of more questions, and it gives two such follow-up questions itself; new questions are a normal part of systematic investigation, not a sign of failure. It also says even the puffing of a puri is not completely understood by scientists today, so questions that stay open are to be expected.
s: Verdict: he is not right
After one round of experiments, more questions are expected
Open questions are normal: even puri puffing is not completely understood

questions.q:
A group's table reads:
Puri | Puffed? | Time to puff
1 | yes | 5 s
2 | no | 8 s
3 | yes | 6 s
Show that the entry for Puri 2 cannot be right as written, and say how such a puri should be recorded.
questions.a: If Puri 2 did not puff, there was no moment at which it puffed, so it cannot have a 'time to puff' of 8 s: the yes/no observation and the measured one contradict each other. Either the 'no' is wrong (it did puff, after 8 s) or the time is wrong. A puri that does not puff should be recorded as 'no' with no time (a dash), with a note of what was seen.
s: A puri that did not puff has no time to puff
So the yes/no entry and the time contradict each other
Correct record: 'no' with no time, plus a note

questions.q:
Three statements about systematic investigation, as the chapter describes it.
Statement 1: Even the everyday puffing of a puri is not completely understood by scientists today.
Statement 2: An observation counts in science only if it is a number that can be measured.
Statement 3: Once one round of experiments is finished, the investigation is complete and no new questions arise.
Which statement or statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Kabir wants to find out whether atta or maida makes a puri puff faster. His lab record reads:
Trial | Flour | Thickness | Oil | Time to puff
1 | atta | 3 mm | hot | 6 s
2 | maida | 3 mm | boiling hot | 3 s
His conclusion: 'Maida puris puff twice as fast as atta puris.'
(a) List everything that changed between Trial 1 and Trial 2.
(b) Why is his conclusion not sound?
(c) He has time for only one more trial today. Decide the conditions for that trial so that, compared with Trial 1, it answers his question about the flour, and say what comparison it will allow.
questions.a: (a) Two things changed: the flour (atta to maida) and the oil temperature (hot to boiling hot). (b) The chapter says to change only one thing at a time while keeping the others the same. Since both flour and oil temperature changed, he cannot tell whether the faster puffing (3 s against 6 s) was due to maida or to the hotter oil. (c) Maida, 3 mm, hot oil, dropped in the same way as Trial 1. Only the flour then differs from Trial 1, so comparing its time with Trial 1's 6 s shows the effect of flour type alone.
s: Part (a): flour and oil temperature both changed
Part (b): two changes at once, so the cause cannot be told
Part (c): maida, 3 mm, hot oil, same way of dropping; compares flour alone with Trial 1

questions.q: Aisha's teacher calls her week of kitchen puri trials a 'systematic investigation'. Which feature of her work best justifies that name?
questions.a: She asked a question, changed things carefully, observed, kept notes
o: She asked a question, changed things carefully, observed, kept notes
She used costly equipment borrowed from a big laboratory in her city
She found the final explanation of why puris puff, ending the question
She fried more than fifty puris in one day without stopping to record

questions.q:
Leela fried puris rolled to 3 mm, all slid in the same way. In hot oil they took 4 seconds on average to puff; in not very hot oil, 12 seconds.
(a) How many times longer did the puris in not very hot oil take?
(b) Leela writes, 'This is true for puris of every thickness.' Why can she not claim this from her trials?
questions.a: (a) 12 / 4 = 3 times longer. (b) She kept the thickness the same (3 mm) in every trial, so her results apply only to 3 mm puris; she did not test other thicknesses, so she has no observations for them.
s: Part (a): 3 times
Part (b): only 3 mm was tested, so the result cannot be extended to other thicknesses

questions.q:
Asha timed puris rolled to the same thickness and slid in the same way, three in each oil, and kept notes.
Oil | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Notes
Boiling hot | 2 s | 3 s | 4 s | oil smoked and splattered; puris browned at the edges
Hot | 5 s | 7 s | 6 s | nothing unusual
Not very hot | 15 s | 13 s | 14 s | puris looked oily
(a) Find the average time to puff for each oil.
(b) Arrange the oils from fastest to slowest average puffing.
(c) Is time to puff a yes/no or a measured observation? What does it let Asha say that a yes/no record could not?
(d) What does the Notes column tell her that the time columns cannot?
(e) Asha's brother says, 'So boiling hot oil is always best for puris.' Judge this claim.
questions.a: (a) Boiling hot (2 + 3 + 4)/3 = 3 s; hot (5 + 7 + 6)/3 = 6 s; not very hot (15 + 13 + 14)/3 = 14 s. (b) Boiling hot, hot, not very hot. (c) Measured (seconds): it shows how much faster one oil was (3 s against 14 s), not just whether the puri puffed. (d) The boiling hot oil smoked and splattered and browned the edges, and the not very hot oil gave oily puris; the times alone show none of this. (e) Not justified. Boiling hot oil was fastest, but the notes show smoke, splattering and browned edges, while hot oil puffed puris in 6 s with nothing unusual; and 'always' goes beyond her trials, which used only one thickness.
s: (a) averages 3 s, 6 s, 14 s
(b) order boiling hot, hot, not very hot
(c) measured; shows how much faster, not just whether
(d) notes show smoking, splattering, browned edges and oily puris
(e) judgement: fastest is not best; notes and one thickness limit the claim

questions.q: A Class 8 group in Lucknow writes: 'We fried nine puris, three each in boiling hot, hot and not very hot oil. We timed each one with a stopwatch. Now we want to find out whether adding a spoon of suji to the dough changes how it puffs.' Identify two habits of systematic investigation that this report shows, quoting the words that show each, and one habit from the chapter that the report does not show.
questions.a: Shows (any two): measuring an observation as a number: 'We timed each one with a stopwatch'; thinking of new questions after one round: 'Now we want to find out whether adding a spoon of suji...'; trying different settings of one thing: 'three each in boiling hot, hot and not very hot oil'. Not shown: keeping notes of everything seen and sensed, such as whether the oil splattered, smelled or smoked (also accept: stating that the other conditions were kept the same).
s: First habit with matching quote
Second habit with matching quote
Missing habit: notes of what was seen and sensed (or other conditions kept the same)

questions.q: True or False? 'An observation does not need a number; "yes, the puri puffed" is a proper observation too.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says some observations have just yes or no answers, such as whether the puri puffs up, while others give a number we can measure, such as the time it takes to puff in seconds. Both kinds are proper observations.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: observations can be yes/no or measured numbers

questions.q:
For their school's Diwali food stall in Indore, a group tests two sizes of dough circle, keeping everything else alike, and records only whether each puri puffs.
Size | Puris fried | Puris that puffed
Small | 10 | 9
Large | 10 | 6
Only puffed puris can be sold: small ones at ₹5 each and large ones at ₹8 each. On the stall day they will have dough for 20 circles of one size only.
(a) Is 'puffed or not' a yes/no or a measured observation? Name a measured observation they could add.
(b) If the same share puffs as in the test, how many puris would puff from 20 small circles, and how many from 20 large ones?
(c) How much money would each choice bring in?
(d) The stall's aim is to earn as much money as possible. Decide which size to make, and say what the group gives up by choosing it.
questions.a: (a) It is a yes/no observation. A measured one: the time each puri takes to puff, in seconds. (b) Small: 20 x 9/10 = 18 puffed. Large: 20 x 6/10 = 12 puffed. (c) Small: 18 x ₹5 = ₹90. Large: 12 x ₹8 = ₹96. (d) Large circles: they bring in ₹96 against ₹90, so they meet the aim, even though 6 fewer puris puff (12 against 18) and more dough is wasted on puris that cannot be sold.
s: Part (a): yes/no; time to puff in seconds as a measured observation
Part (b): 18 small and 12 large
Part (c): ₹90 and ₹96
Part (d): large, as ₹96 is more, giving up 6 puffed puris

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Pranav's note 'the oil splattered when the dough went in' is worth keeping, even though his question was only about puffing.
Reason (R): Some observations have just yes or no answers, while others give a number we can measure.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) A scientist in a laboratory in Bengaluru tests whether the amount of a nutrient changes how fast some microbes grow, measuring their growth every day. Name two steps her work shares with a Class 8 student's kitchen puri trials.
(b) Her laboratory has costly machines. Why does the chapter still count the student's kitchen work as the same kind of science?
questions.a: (a) Any two: both begin with a focused question; both change something they can control and observe or measure the result; both record what they see. (b) The chapter says this is exactly how all scientific experiments, from simple to the most complicated, are done: it is the same systematic investigation, whatever the equipment.
s: Part (a): two shared steps (question, change and measure, record)
Part (b): all experiments, simple or complicated, follow the same systematic way

questions.q:
Neha sketches the Moon on five nights after purnima and writes 'lit part smaller than last night' each time.
(a) Her friend says, 'Sketching the Moon is not science: there is no experiment and no puri.' Reply using the chapter's closing lines.
(b) Write one new question her sketches could lead her to investigate.
questions.a: (a) The chapter ends by saying that whether it is the puffing of a puri or the shrinking bright part of the Moon after purnima, careful observations should guide our explorations. Neha's nightly sketches are exactly such careful observations, so they are part of investigating, even without an experiment. (b) For example: 'After how many nights does the Moon become full again?' or 'Does the lit part shrink by the same amount every night?'
s: Part (a): the chapter names the shrinking Moon after purnima as something careful observation should guide
Part (b): a new question from her observations

questions.q: Design a systematic investigation for the question: 'Does resting the rolled circles for 10 minutes before frying change how they puff?' Your plan must state (a) the two settings you will compare, (b) one yes/no observation and one measured observation you will record, (c) two kinds of notes you will keep while frying, (d) which result would make you say resting helps and which would make you say it does not, and (e) one new question your results might lead to.
questions.a: (a) Circles fried straight after rolling against circles rested for 10 minutes, with everything else done alike. (b) Yes/no: whether each puri puffs. Measured: the time it takes to puff, in seconds. (c) For example: whether the oil splattered, smelled or smoked; whether one side came out thinner or the colour changed. (d) Resting helps if the rested circles puff more often or faster (a shorter average time); it does not if both groups puff about equally often in about the same time. (e) For example: 'Does resting for 30 minutes make a bigger difference?'
s: (a) rested and not-rested circles as the two settings
(b) one yes/no and one measured observation
(c) two kinds of notes, such as splatter, smell, smoke
(d) results that would and would not show an effect
(e) a sensible new question

questions.q: A group wants to see the effect of boiling hot, hot and not very hot oil on puffing. Which plan follows the chapter's advice on changing conditions?
questions.a: Same-thickness circles, dropped the same way, into the three oils
o: Same-thickness circles, dropped the same way, into the three oils
Thin dough in boiling hot oil, thick in hot, thicker in not very hot
Atta dough in boiling hot oil and maida dough in the other two oils
All dough into hot oil, with a different thickness for each circle

questions.q:
Two friends time the same puri. Jaya starts her stopwatch when the dough touches the oil; Kabir starts his when the dough rises to the surface. Both stop when the puri is fully puffed. Jaya reads 7 s and Kabir reads 4 s.
(a) Why do their times differ, though they watched the same puri?
(b) What must the group agree on before the next round so that all their times can be compared?
questions.a: (a) They started timing at different moments: Jaya's 7 s includes the 3 s before the dough rose to the surface, which Kabir did not count. (b) One fixed rule for when to start and stop the stopwatch (for example, start when the dough touches the oil and stop when it is fully puffed), used for every puri by everyone.
